topic: Why 'warm' (orange) light has a LOWER color temperature than 'cool' (blue) light: black-body physics runs opposite to the aesthetic labels. Hotter glow = shorter peak wavelength (Wien's law): candle 1,850 K orange, daylight 6,500 K white, a 3,000 K filament peaks in infrared at 966 nm, the Sun (~5,800 K) near 500 nm.

youtube.title: Warm Light Is the COOLER Light (Why Low Kelvin = Orange)
youtube.description:
The 'warm' orange light on your camera's Kelvin scale is the lower-temperature light. Heat any object until it glows and its color depends on how hot it is: roughly 1,000 K looks red, a candle flame (about 1,850 K) orange, daylight (about 6,500 K) white, and hotter still shifts toward blue. Wien's displacement law (peak wavelength = 2,898 um*K / T) explains it: about 5,800 K peaks near 500 nm (the Sun), while 3,000 K peaks near 966 nm, in the infrared. 'Warm' and 'cool' describe how a color feels, not its temperature, so the physics runs the opposite way. The colors and curves are computed from Planck's law for an ideal black body; real lamps are approximations.
